SECTION I
L	The first time, the intention was simply to find a place that was quiet, but not somnolent. A
town rather than a village. There had to be activity to observe. A few tourists, but only a few.
Not too many people like myself. That was the plan, if it could be called a plan. During the
stay, I would put my thoughts in order. I had pictured where this procedure would be carried
out: a small square, the focal point, with café tables in the shade of a huge plane tree, an
assortment of shops, whitewashed walls, the small hotel in which I would stay. At all times of
day, encounters would occur there. In the evening, dozens would congregate.
The most popular resorts in the vicinity were to the east of the airport, and so were the
nearest historical sites of significance. Drive north and I would be leaving the sea behind — the
sea was a prerequisite; sand was not. To the south lay the city, then the bay. Therefore, it had
to be west, initially. I followed the coast, and the road turned south.
An hour later: a small town of immediate potential — optimum size, and open to the sea.
Tables on the waterfront. No English overheard in the course of a meander through the
streets. On the other side of the headland, a long and almost unpopulated beach — ideal for
solitude, which would at some point be required. The main square, though, was not suitable:
what I had imagined was a space in the centre of a town, through which everyone would pass,
but this was not in the centre, and its café was no place for lingering.
Source: An extract from One Boat by Jonathan Buckley

questions.stimulus:
I.	It seemed an unlikely choice, this large establishment in the financial district, so that I stood
outside and checked the address, the name of the restaurant, I wondered if I had made a
mistake. But then I saw him through the window, seated at a table toward the back of the
dining room. I stared through the layers of glass and reflection, the frame of my own face.
Something uncoiled in my stomach, slow and languorous, and I decided it would be better if I
left now, and did not go in to him.
At that moment, the front door opened and a man stepped out, he inclined his head and held
the door open, and because of that small courtesy: an invitation or injunction to enter: I went
inside. The foyer was busy with diners collecting their coats, people surging in and then out of
the entryway, and briefly I allowed myself to be buffeted by their movement. When the crowd
dispersed, I could see across the dining room floor again, he was bent over the menu,
examining it in a nervous posture. His table was between the entrance to the kitchen and the
bathrooms, caught in a stream of constant traffic. A pair of businessmen bumped against its
edge and he sat back impatiently, I saw him take a deep breath, as if trying to collect or steady
his thoughts.
The host asked if I had a reservation. I said that I was meeting someone and indicated the
young man seated at the back of the restaurant. Xavier. It occurred to me that the host must
have been the person to seat him at this inhospitable table, and I saw a flicker of surprise
cross his features as I pointed. He looked quickly from my face to my coat to my jewellery. It
was my age, above all. That was the thing that confounded him. He gave a tight smile and
asked me to please follow him. I was under no obligation to obey, I could tell the host that I
had made a mistake, or that something had come up, I could turn and slip away. But by that
point it seemed too late, and much as I had entered at the behest of the man at the door,
according to the imperative of mere courtesy, I followed the host through the warren of tables,
each one occupied. I wondered again why Xavier had chosen such a crowded venue at such a
busy time, when we might just as easily have met elsewhere, in the afternoon, in the morning

or early evening, for a coffee or quiet drink. The din pressed against me, crowding the inside of
my head so that it was hard to think, difficult to locate my thoughts amidst the noise.
Source: An extract from Audition by Katie Kitamura

outside and checked the address, the name of the restaurant, I wondered if I had made a
mistake. But then I saw him through the window, seated at a table toward the back of the
dining room. I stared through the layers of glass and reflection, the frame of my own face.
Something uncoiled in my stomach, slow and languorous, and I decided it would be better if I
left now, and did not go in to him.
At that moment, the front door opened and a man stepped out, he inclined his head and held
the door open, and because of that small courtesy: an invitation or injunction to enter: I went
inside. The foyer was busy with diners collecting their coats, people surging in and then out of
the entryway, and briefly I allowed myself to be buffeted by their movement. When the crowd
dispersed, I could see across the dining room floor again, he was bent over the menu,
examining it in a nervous posture. His table was between the entrance to the kitchen and the
bathrooms, caught in a stream of constant traffic. A pair of businessmen bumped against its
edge and he sat back impatiently, I saw him take a deep breath, as if trying to collect or steady
his thoughts.
The host asked if I had a reservation. I said that I was meeting someone and indicated the
young man seated at the back of the restaurant. Xavier. It occurred to me that the host must
have been the person to seat him at this inhospitable table, and I saw a flicker of surprise
cross his features as I pointed. He looked quickly from my face to my coat to my jewellery. It
was my age, above all. That was the thing that confounded him. He gave a tight smile and
asked me to please follow him. I was under no obligation to obey, I could tell the host that I
had made a mistake, or that something had come up, I could turn and slip away. But by that
point it seemed too late, and much as I had entered at the behest of the man at the door,
according to the imperative of mere courtesy, I followed the host through the warren of tables,
each one occupied. I wondered again why Xavier had chosen such a crowded venue at such a
busy time, when we might just as easily have met elsewhere, in the afternoon, in the morning

or early evening, for a coffee or quiet drink. The din pressed against me, crowding the inside of
my head so that it was hard to think, difficult to locate my thoughts amidst the noise.

questions.stimulus:
Il.	The day was flat. That morning his mind had abandoned him and left his body wandering
down below. The empty body went listlessly through its routine, pale and vacant-eyed under
the fluorescent strip lights, as his soul floated above the aisles and thought only of tomorrow.
Tomorrow was something to look forward to.
Shuggie was methodical in setting up for his shift. All the pots of oily dips and spreads were
decanted into clean trays. The edges were wiped free of any splashes that would go brown
quickly and ruin the illusion of freshness. The sliced hams were artfully arranged with fake
parsley sprigs, and the olives were turned so that the viscous juice slid like mucus over their
green skins.
Ann McGee had the brass neck to call in sick again that morning, leaving him with the
thankless task of running his deli counter and her rotisserie stand all alone. No day ever

started well with six dozen raw chickens, and today of all days, it was stealing the sweetness
out of his daydreams.
He pushed industrial skewers through each cold, dead bird and lined them up neatly in a row.
They sat there, with their stubby wings crossed over their fat little chests like so many
headless babies. There was a time he would have taken pride in this orderliness. In reality,
pushing the metal through the bumpy pink flesh was the easy part; the difficult part was
resisting the urge to do the same to the customers. They would pore over the hot glass and
study each of the carcasses in detail. They would choose only the best bird, ignorant to the fact
that battery farming meant they were all identical. Shuggie would stand there, his back teeth
pinching the inside of his cheek, and indulge their indecisiveness with a forced smile. Then the
pantomime would really begin. “Gies three breasts, five thighs, and just wan wing the day,
son.”
Source: An extract from Shuggie Bain by Douglas Stuart

VI.	World Obesity Atlas 2026: Childhood obesity is rising at an unprecedented rate, making it
the focus of the World Obesity Atlas 2026. The prevalence of obesity among school-age children
has increased from 4% in 1975 to nearly 20% in 2022, and the fastest increases are in low- and
middle-income countries where most of the world’s children live. For the first time in history,
more children globally will be living with obesity than with underweight.
The data in this World Obesity Atlas 2026 presents a comprehensive and urgent picture of the
scale, distribution and projected trajectory of childhood obesity. It includes new global,
regional, and national estimates of children living with overweight and obesity, along with
projections extending to 2040. It also provides updated figures on the number of children
already exhibiting early signs of heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and liver disease as a result of
excess weight. In addition, it assesses national performance across seven indicators measuring
children’s exposure to obesity risk factors and evaluates how countries are performing on
seven key policies designed to protect children from obesity. Finally, the Atlas includes 196
national scorecards detailing country-level data to inform local advocacy and action.
Historically, the prevalence of obesity was highest in high-income countries. This is no longer
the case as prevalence has risen rapidly in upper-middle-income countries. Low- and lower-

middle-income countries continue to have lower prevalence levels (compared to high- and
upper-middle-income countries) but nearly 50% of children and adolescents who live with
obesity will reside in these countries by 2040 and over 85% in low- and middle-income
countries.

(Samajwadi Party). The mandate of the committee is to examine such cases and “make such
recommendations as it may deem fit”. It can call the relevant people as part of its examination
and look at related documents. It has to then make a report and if the Council has not fixed
any time for its presentation, the report shall be presented within one month of the date on
which reference to the Committee was made. www.lawpreptutorial.com

suggested. The Chairman or any member of the Committee or any other member can move
that the Council agrees, disagrees, or agrees with amendments, with the recommendations
contained in the report. A large number of notices are rejected, with penal action recommended

IX.	Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh Plan Social Media Ban for Minors: Karnataka has
announced a ban on social media use by children under 16 in its latest Budget, and Andhra
Pradesh is moving to introduce a measure that would prohibit the use of such services — a
signal of the growing momentum in India to protect children from the various harms that
social media platforms can cause.
With the objective of preventing adverse effects of increasing mobile usage in children, usage of
social media will be banned for children under the age of 16,” Karnataka Chief Minister
Siddaramaiah stated while presenting the state’s annual Budget. He did not offer technical
details of how such a ban would be implemented. Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N
Chandrababu Naidu stated that the state will introduce similar regulations within 90 days.

Calls for banning social media use for children are gaining traction across the world that went
into effect last year. During his keynote address at the India-AI Impact Summit last month,
French President Emmanuel Macron called on India to consider banning social media for
children.
Though India is yet to make a regulatory move at the central level, preliminary discussions
around age-based social media restrictions are learnt to have begun at the IT Ministry. Last
month, the Centre was discussing age-based restrictions with social media companies.
It also stated that simpler devices, such as basic phones or education-only tablets, should be
promoted among children along with enforced usage limits and content filters.
There are, according to tech executives, operational challenges in implementing state-level
bans.

questions.stimulus:
XI.	The terms 'wager' or 'wagering agreement' are not defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
However, Section 30 of the Act explicitly declares that agreements by way of wager are void. A
wagering agreement is one where two parties holding opposite views touching the issue of a
future uncertain event mutually agree that dependent on the determination of that event, one
shall pay or hand over to him, a sum of money or other stake. Neither party must have any
other interest in that contract than the sum or stake he will win or lose, and there must be no
other real consideration for the making of such contract by either of the parties. If either of the
parties may win but cannot lose, or may lose but cannot win, it is not a wagering contract. The
essence of a wager is that each side should stand to win or lose, depending on the uncertain
event. In India, wagering agreements are void ab initio, meaning they have no legal effect
from the beginning. This renders them unenforceable in a court of law. Even Section 65, which
deals with the obligation of a person who has received advantage under a void agreement to
restore it, is not applicable to wagering agreements because they are void ab initio. However,
it is important to distinguish between void and illegal agreements. Agreements by way of
wager are void but not illegal, except in states like Maharashtra and Gujarat where they have
been made illegal by local statutes. This means that while the main wagering transaction is
void, collateral transactions to a wager are generally enforceable.
Source: "Exceptions to a Wagering Agreement and its Enforceability in India: An Analysis." Jus
Corpus Law Journal, Published December 27, 2021.

questions.stimulus:
XI.	The terms 'wager' or 'wagering agreement' are not defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
However, Section 30 of the Act explicitly declares that agreements by way of wager are void. A
wagering agreement is one where two parties holding opposite views touching the issue of a
future uncertain event mutually agree that dependent on the determination of that event, one
shall pay or hand over to him, a sum of money or other stake. Neither party must have any
other interest in that contract than the sum or stake he will win or lose, and there must be no
other real consideration for the making of such contract by either of the parties. If either of the
parties may win but cannot lose, or may lose but cannot win, it is not a wagering contract. The
essence of a wager is that each side should stand to win or lose, depending on the uncertain
event. In India, wagering agreements are void ab initio, meaning they have no legal effect
from the beginning. This renders them unenforceable in a court of law. Even Section 65, which
deals with the obligation of a person who has received advantage under a void agreement to
restore it, is not applicable to wagering agreements because they are void ab initio. However,
it is important to distinguish between void and illegal agreements. Agreements by way of
wager are void but not illegal, except in states like Maharashtra and Gujarat where they have
been made illegal by local statutes. This means that while the main wagering transaction is
void, collateral transactions to a wager are generally enforceable.
Source: "Exceptions to a Wagering Agreement and its Enforceability in India: An Analysis." Jus
Corpus Law Journal, Published December 27, 2021.

XII. "The doctrine of Rule of Law, first propounded by A.V. Dicey in his seminal 1885 work
Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution, remains one of the most enduring
foundations of modern constitutional democracies. It has travelled through centuries, crossing
borders and adapting to various legal cultures. In India, though rooted in a written
Constitution rather than unwritten conventions like the UK, the Rule of Law has become both
a constitutional precept and a moral imperative. Dicey's Rule of Law rests on three pillars:
First, Supremacy of law, meaning no man is above the law. Second, Equality before the law,
meaning every person is subject to the ordinary law of the land administered by ordinary
courts. And third, Predominance of legal spirit, meaning constitutional principles arise from
judicial decisions securing individual liberties. In India, the rule of law implies that the
Constitution is supreme and all the three organs of the government, viz. legislature, executive
and judiciary are subordinate to and have to act in consonance with the Constitution.
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, the Supreme Court held that Rule of Law
constitutes one of the basic features of the Constitution. The Court has also observed that the
rule of law runs like a golden thread through every provision of the Constitution (see Som Raj
v. State of Haryana). Furthermore, the concept excludes the existence of arbitrariness, of
prerogative or even wide discretionary power on the part of the government. Dicey observed
that wherever there is discretion, there is room for arbitrariness. Thus, in a government based
on principles of law and not of men, even the highest executive authority is bound by the law
of the land."

XIII. Intergenerational equity is a foundational principle in environmental law that emphasizes the
duty of the current generation to preserve the environment for future generations. It is based
on the idea that those who have received the environment in pristine form are under an
obligation to maintain it in that state for generations to come. This principle has three main
components: conservation of options, which means preserving biodiversity and genetic
resources; conservation of quality, which involves sustaining environmental quality; and
conservation of access, which ensures equitable access to resources for all generations. The
principle aims to balance environmental protection with development activities between
present and future generations. In international law, it finds support in the 1972 Stockholm
Declaration and the 1992 Rio Declaration, which state that the right to development must be
fulfilled equitably for present as well as future generations. In India, the Supreme Court has
recognised intergenerational equity as part of sustainable development, holding that the
present generation owes a duty to future generations to keep the environment clean. The
principle requires replacing short-term decisions with long-term responsibility, supported by
public participation, legal frameworks, and planning. It serves as a mechanism to prevent
excessive exploitation of natural resources and maintain ecological balance.
Source: "Intergenerational Equity in Environmental Law," The Academic Journal (2026).

questions.stimulus:
XIV. When two or more persons are jointly responsible for causing damage to a third party, they are
known as joint tortfeasors. Under the traditional common law rule, the liability of joint
tortfeasors was joint and several, meaning that each tortfeasor could be held liable for the
entire damage suffered by the plaintiff. This allowed the injured party to recover full
compensation from any one of the wrongdoers, irrespective of their individual degree of fault.
While this rule protected the plaintiffs right to effective compensation, it often resulted in
hardship where one tortfeasor bore the entire financial burden despite others being equally or
more at fault.www.lawpreptutorial.com
To address this imbalance, the doctrine of contribution was developed. Contribution permits a
tortfeasor who has paid more than their fair share of damages to recover proportionate
amounts from other joint tortfeasors, based on their relative degree of fault. The doctrine is
founded on principles of equity and fairness, ensuring that liability is shared according to
responsibility and that no party is unjustly enriched at the expense of another.
Indemnity, in contrast, involves a complete transfer of liability from one party to another. It
usually arises where one tortfeasor is only secondarily or vicariously liable, while the other is
primarily responsible for the wrongful act. Common examples include an employer
indemnifying an employee for acts done in the course of employment, or a manufacturer
indemnifying a retailer for losses caused by a defective product. Unlike contribution,
indemnity often flows from contractual terms or special legal relationships.

In India, various common law principles recognize the principle of contribution where several
persons are liable for the same act. Indian courts have further evolved rules for apportionment
based on comparative negligence. Both doctrines operate only after the plaintiff has been fully
compensated, thereby balancing the interests of justice, fairness, and efficient risk allocation.
Source: G. R. J., "Torts - Indemnification of Joint Tortfeasor Constructively Liable -
Contribution and Indemnity Between Joint Tortfeasors," Louisiana Law Review, Volume 4,
Number 3 (March 1942), pp. 475-479.

questions.stimulus:
XVI. India's expansion of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPJ), particularly through platforms like
UPI and Bhashini, has been hailed as a global model for financial inclusion and linguistic
accessibility. However, as the state pivots toward "Data-Led Governance," a critical ethical
divide has emerged. The premise of DPI is that by digitizing citizen data, the government can
deliver services with unprecedented precision, cutting through the red tape of traditional
bureaucracy.
The friction point lies in the concept of "informed consent." In a country with varying levels of
digital literacy, the act of clicking "I Agree" on a government portal often lacks substantive
understanding. Furthermore, the aggregation of health, financial, and biometric data under a
single digital identity creates a "honey pot" for cyber-attacks and potential state surveillance.
Proponents argue that the collective benefit of efficient welfare delivery outweighs individual
privacy concerns in a developing economy. Yet, this utilitarian calculus ignores the fact that

privacy is not a luxury for the elite but a safeguard for the marginalized against
administrative overreach. As we integrate AI into this infrastructure to predict citizen needs,
the risk of "algorithmic bias"—where historical prejudices are coded into service delivery—
becomes a tangible threat to equity.
Source: htips:/ /www.publicationsdivision.nic.in/journals/Journalarchives/Yojana/ Yojana-
English/2024/February/

accessibility. However, as the state pivots toward "Data-Led Governance," a critical ethical

deliver services with unprecedented precision, cutting through the red tape of traditional
bureaucracy.

digital literacy, the act of clicking "I Agree" on a government portal often lacks substantive
understanding. Furthermore, the aggregation of health, financial, and biometric data under a
single digital identity creates a "honey pot" for cyber-attacks and potential state surveillance.

privacy concerns in a developing economy. Yet, this utilitarian calculus ignores the fact that

privacy is not a luxury for the elite but a safeguard for the marginalized against
administrative overreach. As we integrate AI into this infrastructure to predict citizen needs,
the risk of "algorithmic bias"—where historical prejudices are coded into service delivery—
becomes a tangible threat to equity.

XVII. In early 2026, a landmark case reached the Supreme Court where a group of youth activists
sued the government for what they described as “intergenerational climate injustice.” The
petitioners argued that the state’s continued reliance on coal-fired power plants, despite the
existence of viable green alternatives, violates the fundamental right to a clean environment
for future generations. According to the petitioners, the environmental harm caused by
present-day policy choices will be borne primarily by citizens of tomorrow, who have no
representation in current decision-making processes. This controversy brings to the fore the
legal doctrine of the “Public Trust,” which posits that the state is not the owner of natural
resources but merely a trustee holding them for the benefit of the public, including those yet to
be born.
Opponents of such climate litigation, however, strongly contest this approach. They argue that
courts are ill-equipped to handle “polycentric” issues, namely problems that involve complex
and interconnected economic, social, and technical trade-offs. In their view, decisions relating
to energy policy should remain the exclusive domain of the legislature and executive, as these
institutions are democratically accountable and better positioned to assess competing public
interests. They warn that a judicial mandate directing the shutdown of coal-fired power plants
could result in immediate energy shortages, thereby affecting millions of current citizens who
rely on affordable power for their livelihoods and daily needs.
At this juncture, the “precautionary principle”’—which supports taking preventive measures to
avoid future harm even when scientific certainty is incomplete—comes into direct conflict with
the “necessity of development.” The court must now determine whether the “Constitution of
today” can adequately protect the “citizens of tomorrow” without the judiciary overstepping its
institutional boundaries or encroaching upon the functions of the other branches of
government.

climate-case-file-fresh-legal-action-against-their-state-government/

XVIII. The rise of the gig economy in India has redefined the traditional employer-employee
relationship. Millions of workers now operate through digital platforms as “partners” rather
than “employees,” a semantic shift that carries profound legal consequences. This
classification allows platforms to bypass traditional labour laws, such as those mandating
minimum wage, provident fund, and health insurance. The platforms argue that they provide
“unrivaled flexibility,” allowing workers to be their own bosses and choose their own hours—a
luxury not afforded by the 9-to-5 grind. www.lawpreptutorial.com
However, critics argue that this “flexibility” is often a mirage. In reality,
workers are often controlled by opaque algorithms that determine their earnings, work
distribution, and even account suspension. This “algorithmic management” creates a power
imbalance where the worker has the liabilities of an independent contractor but the
constraints of an employee. The debate has now reached the legislature, with proposals to
create a “third category” of workers who are neither full employees nor purely independent
contractors. The challenge lies in crafting a law that provides a “social safety net” without
stifling the innovation and low-cost services that define the platform economy.

XVIII. The rise of the gig economy in India has redefined the traditional employer-employee
relationship. Millions of workers now operate through digital platforms as “partners” rather
than “employees,” a semantic shift that carries profound legal consequences. This
classification allows platforms to bypass traditional labour laws, such as those mandating
minimum wage, provident fund, and health insurance. The platforms argue that they provide
“unrivaled flexibility,” allowing workers to be their own bosses and choose their own hours—a
luxury not afforded by the 9-to-5 grind. www.lawpreptutorial.com
However, critics argue that this “flexibility” is often a mirage. In reality,
workers are often controlled by opaque algorithms that determine their earnings, work
distribution, and even account suspension. This “algorithmic management” creates a power
imbalance where the worker has the liabilities of an independent contractor but the
constraints of an employee. The debate has now reached the legislature, with proposals to
create a “third category” of workers who are neither full employees nor purely independent
contractors. The challenge lies in crafting a law that provides a “social safety net” without
stifling the innovation and low-cost services that define the platform economy.
